blocks.text: 我们最新的模型进展为 COBOL、Fortran 和 Visual Basic 等低资源编程语言的软件构建与迁移带来了更强的能力。与 Python 和 JavaScript 等语言相比，这些语言可供模型学习的代码和文档更少，但它们支撑着全球关键基础设施和基本服务。COBOL 支撑着⁠（在新窗口中打开）超过 40% 的网上银行系统、80% 的线下信用卡交易和 95% 的 ATM 交易，而 Fortran 被用于天气预报⁠（在新窗口中打开）和核反应堆安全分析⁠（在新窗口中打开）。提升 AI 在这些语言上的工作能力，可以帮助团队维护和现代化基本服务所依赖的软件。

blocks.text: 这项工作以开发者和企业客户的反馈为指导，他们告诉我们，编码模型在这些语言上往往表现不佳。维护和现代化这类软件可能很困难：文档可能不完整，最初的开发者可能已经离开公司，重要的业务规则可能只存在于代码中。无论团队是在修复缺陷还是迁移到另一种语言，他们都需要保留系统所依赖的行为。

blocks.text: 为了衡量进展，我们开发了两项评估。MultiLangBench 测试模型能否在 20 种不同的编程语言中从零构建一个兼容 SQLite 的数据库引擎。我们的 COBOL 迁移评估测试模型能否将现有程序迁移到另一种语言，同时保留其行为。两者共同测试了两项互补的技能：构建新软件，以及保留现有软件的行为。

blocks.text: 在 MultiLangBench 上，GPT‑6 Astra 在 20 种编程语言中平均测试通过率达到 87.4%，高于 GPT‑5.6 Sol 的 26.8%，且所有测试语言均有提升。GPT‑6 Luna 也优于 GPT‑5.6 Sol，达到 40.3%，同时估计 API 成本降低约 78%。

blocks.text: 1. 从零构建 SQLite（MultiLangBench）

inlines.text: 1. 从零构建 SQLite（MultiLangBench）

blocks.text: MultiLangBench 要求模型用指定的编程语言构建一个兼容 SQLite 的数据库引擎。模型必须组织代码库、管理状态、处理错误，并在保留现有功能的同时添加新功能。

inlines.text: MultiLangBench 要求模型用指定的编程语言构建一个兼容 SQLite 的数据库引擎。模型必须组织代码库、管理状态、处理错误，并在保留现有功能的同时添加新功能。

blocks.text: 为了跨语言比较实现，我们使用数据库文件作为共享接口。候选程序接收一个初始数据库和一条 SQL 查询，然后生成一个修改后的数据库。我们使用参考 SQLite 实现来检查生成的数据库是否具有预期内容。这使我们能够应用相同的测试，无论构建引擎使用的是哪种语言。

blocks.text: 在最高推理强度下，GPT‑6 Astra 在 20 种语言上的平均测试通过率达到 87.4%，高于 GPT‑5.6 Sol 的 26.8%。所有受测语言均有提升，包括 COBOL（10.9% 至 72.1%）、OCaml（25.6% 至 85.8%）、Fortran（21.4% 至 83.5%）和 Visual Basic（27.5% 至 89.4%）。Astra 在 20 种语言中的 19 种得分超过 83%，COBOL 仍是最难的，为 72%。

blocks.text: GPT‑6 Luna 提供了一种成本更低的选项，在所有受测语言上也均优于 GPT‑5.6 Sol。在最高推理强度下，其平均测试通过率达到 40.3%。提升包括 COBOL（10.9% 至 17.1%）、OCaml（25.6% 至 34.1%）、Fortran（21.4% 至 31.4%）和 Visual Basic（27.5% 至 41.6%）。这些改进的估计平均 API 成本为每个样本 $0.77，而 GPT‑5.6 Sol 为 $3.48，约低 78%。

blocks.text: 2. 迁移 COBOL 代码库

inlines.text: 2. 迁移 COBOL 代码库

blocks.text: 我们的第二项评估要求模型将 COBOL 程序迁移到 C++、Java、Kotlin、Python 或 Rust，同时保留每个程序的功能。

inlines.text: 我们的第二项评估要求模型将 COBOL 程序迁移到 C++、Java、Kotlin、Python 或 Rust，同时保留每个程序的功能。

blocks.text: 成功的迁移需要理解程序的业务逻辑和 COBOL 的特定语言行为。COBOL 程序通常处理金融交易和业务记录，其中舍入规则和缺失记录处理等细节反映了业务需求。例如，COBOL 的定点算术会丢弃多余的小数位，除非明确要求舍入。若重写时改为对这些值进行舍入，可能运行无错误，却产生不同的财务结果。

Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)

blocks.text: Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL supports⁠(opens in a new window) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in weather forecasting⁠(opens in a new window) and nuclear reactor safety analysis⁠(opens in a new window). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.

blocks.text: This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.

blocks.text: To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does.

blocks.text: 1. Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)

inlines.text: 1. Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)

blocks.text: MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

inlines.text: MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

blocks.text: To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.

blocks.text: 2. Migrating a COBOL codebase

inlines.text: 2. Migrating a COBOL codebase

blocks.text: Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

inlines.text: Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

blocks.text: Successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.

blocks.text: To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.
